# Frequency–severity alternatives

Separate models help investigate whether a pricing discrepancy comes from how
often claims occur (frequency) or how much each claim costs (severity). For example,
a segment may have more claims than predicted but smaller claims than predicted;
the product can conceal these opposing errors. Use the component tables to choose
what to investigate, then assess the final pure premium against losses as well.

These two alternatives use the same stored partition as the direct Tweedie models.
Frequency fits claim count / exposure with exposure weights. Severity fits
claim amount / claim count with claim-count weights on positive-claim rows only;
that filter remains inside `FrequencySeverityModel.fit`. Their product predicts
pure-premium rates. The GLMs use the tariff structure; the GBMs use raw features.
Good calibration of each component in its own groups does not guarantee calibration
of their product on all policies: the weights and populations differ, and component
errors can reinforce or offset each other.

{{< include _shared.qmd >}}

```{python}
#| include: false

portfolio = load_portfolio()
glm_config, gbm_config = make_experiment_configs(str(PORTFOLIO_PATH))
glm_run = run_experiment(glm_config)
gbm_run = run_experiment(gbm_config)
runs = [glm_run, gbm_run]
train_frame = portfolio.iloc[list(glm_run.train_indices)].copy()
test_frame = portfolio.iloc[list(glm_run.test_indices)].copy()
y_train = train_frame["claim_amount"].to_numpy()
w_train = train_frame["exposure"].to_numpy()
y_test = test_frame["claim_amount"].to_numpy()
w_test = test_frame["exposure"].to_numpy()
raw_predict_columns = [*FEATURES, "exposure"]
```

## Fit the two alternatives

The configurations keep the earlier GLM preprocessing and GBM settings. Severity's
positive-claim training filter remains inside the composite estimator; no rows are
removed from the frequency training population.

```{python}
fs_glm_config = glm_config.model_copy(update={
    "name": "fremtpl2-frequency-severity-glm",
    "models": {
        "frequency-severity-glm": ModelSpec(
            kind="frequency_severity",
            frequency=ModelSpec(
                kind="glm",
                params={"family": "poisson", "link": "log", "alpha": 0.001},
            ),
            severity=ModelSpec(
                kind="glm",
                params={"family": "gamma", "link": "log", "alpha": 0.001},
            ),
        ),
    },
})
fs_gbm_config = gbm_config.model_copy(update={
    "name": "fremtpl2-frequency-severity-gbm",
    "models": {
        "frequency-severity-gbm": ModelSpec(
            kind="frequency_severity",
            frequency=ModelSpec(
                kind="gbm",
                params={
                    "objective": "poisson",
                    "n_estimators": 100,
                    "num_leaves": 31,
                    "learning_rate": 0.05,
                    "random_state": RANDOM_STATE,
                },
            ),
            severity=ModelSpec(
                kind="gbm",
                params={
                    "objective": "gamma",
                    "n_estimators": 100,
                    "num_leaves": 31,
                    "learning_rate": 0.05,
                    "random_state": RANDOM_STATE,
                },
            ),
        ),
    },
})
```

```{python}
#| include: false
appendix_runs = []
fs_estimators = {}
for config in [fs_glm_config, fs_gbm_config]:
    run, fitted = run_experiment(config, return_estimators=True)
    assert run.data_fingerprint == glm_run.data_fingerprint
    assert run.train_indices == glm_run.train_indices
    assert run.test_indices == glm_run.test_indices
    appendix_runs.append(run)
    fs_estimators.update(fitted)
```

## Read the components for the same policies

Prediction needs features and exposure, with no claim outcomes. For the GLM, reuse
the training-fitted preprocessing before accessing `freq_` and `sev_` on the final
estimator. [Pipeline slicing](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/compose.html#pipeline)
retains those fitted steps; calling `transform` does not refit their bins or groups.
Both components then receive only the transformed features, just as during fitting.
The GBM components receive the raw features.

```{python}
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

component_predictions = {}
component_inputs = test_frame[raw_predict_columns]
for name, estimator in fs_estimators.items():
    if isinstance(estimator, Pipeline):
        component_frame = estimator[:-1].transform(component_inputs)[FEATURES]
        composite = estimator[-1]
    else:
        component_frame = component_inputs[FEATURES]
        composite = estimator
    frequency = np.asarray(composite.freq_.predict(component_frame))
    severity = np.asarray(composite.sev_.predict(component_frame))
    product = frequency * severity
    assert np.isfinite(frequency).all() and (frequency > 0).all()
    assert np.isfinite(severity).all() and (severity > 0).all()
    np.testing.assert_allclose(product, estimator.predict(component_inputs))
    component_predictions[name] = pd.DataFrame({
        "policy_id": test_frame["policy_id"].to_numpy(),
        "frequency": frequency,
        "severity": severity,
        "raw_product": product,
    })
    print(name)
    display(component_predictions[name].head(5).rename(columns={
        "policy_id": "Policy ID", "frequency": "Claims / insured year",
        "severity": "Cost / claim", "raw_product": "Raw cost / insured year",
    }))
```

Multiplying claims per insured year by cost per claim gives cost per insured year.
These are raw component predictions. Later, a training O/P multiplier adjusts the
**product once**. Applying it to both components would multiply the product by the
square of that factor and would give the components an unsupported interpretation.

## Check each component on held-out observations

`calibration_table` sums observed totals and divides by the supplied weights.
For frequency, pass **counts**, predicted frequency, and exposure on **all** test
policies. For severity, pass **amounts**, predicted cost per claim, and claim counts
on **positive-claim** test policies. Zero-claim policies have no observed claim size;
they still receive severity predictions above and remain in product evaluation.

Each table uses five weighted prediction groups (fewer if predictions tie). Frequency
groups have roughly equal exposure; severity groups have roughly equal claim counts.
Group numbers run from lower to higher predictions within that component/model,
so the same number across tables need not identify the same policies. The renamed
columns below show the component units instead of the function's default loss labels.
O/P above one means observed totals exceed predicted totals; below one means the reverse.

```{python}
claim_counts = test_frame["claim_count"].to_numpy()
positive_claim = claim_counts > 0
component_tables = {}
for name, predictions in component_predictions.items():
    frequency_table = calibration_table(
        claim_counts, predictions["frequency"], w_test, n_bins=5,
    ).rename(columns={
        "group": "Group", "exposure": "Exposure (insured years)",
        "claim_amount": "Observed claims", "predicted_claim_amount": "Predicted claims",
        "observed_pure_premium": "Observed claims / year",
        "predicted_pure_premium": "Predicted claims / year", "o_p_ratio": "O/P",
    })
    severity_table = calibration_table(
        y_test[positive_claim], predictions["severity"].to_numpy()[positive_claim],
        claim_counts[positive_claim], n_bins=5,
    ).rename(columns={
        "group": "Group", "exposure": "Claim count",
        "claim_amount": "Observed amount", "predicted_claim_amount": "Predicted amount",
        "observed_pure_premium": "Observed cost / claim",
        "predicted_pure_premium": "Predicted cost / claim", "o_p_ratio": "O/P",
    })
    component_tables[name] = {"frequency": frequency_table, "severity": severity_table}
    print(f"{name}: raw frequency, all held-out policies")
    display(frequency_table.round(3))
    print(f"{name}: raw severity, positive-claim held-out policies")
    display(severity_table.round(3))
```

In the default full-portfolio render (133,535 held-out policies), GLM severity
group 1 contains 1,048 claims: observed cost per claim is about 2,005 versus 1,624
predicted, giving O/P 1.234. Observed claim size is 23.4% above the prediction in
that group, even though the GLM's frequency-group ratios are fairly close to one.
This points to claim-size calibration as a useful next investigation.

For the GBM, severity group 1 has 1,047 claims and observed cost per claim about
2,096 versus 1,437 predicted (O/P 1.458). Its lowest-frequency group instead has
475 observed claims versus about 576 predicted over 14,102 insured years (O/P
0.825). That is an overprediction of claim counts alongside an underprediction
of claim size in a different grouping. The group memberships differ, so these
two ratios cannot be multiplied to explain the product's error. Inspect which
policies and features drive each discrepancy before deciding what to change.
These numbers describe the default run; use the tables above if you change the sample.

Small claim counts and a few large losses can make a severity discrepancy unstable.
Inspect the support columns before deciding to change a feature or model. These
held-out tables diagnose the fitted alternatives; do not use their O/P ratios to
recalibrate predictions on this same holdout.

## Compare the product with direct Tweedie

The raw product is checked against each saved run below. Each alternative also gets
its own multiplier from **training** observed losses divided by training predicted
losses. This balances training totals; it need not improve held-out calibration or
deviance. Gini measures ranking and is unchanged by a positive multiplier.

```{python}
appendix_rows = []
for run in appendix_runs:
    for name in run.models:
        estimator = fs_estimators[name]
        train_prediction = np.asarray(estimator.predict(train_frame[raw_predict_columns]))
        prediction = np.asarray(estimator.predict(test_frame[raw_predict_columns]))
        assert np.isfinite(train_prediction).all() and (train_prediction > 0).all()
        assert np.isfinite(prediction).all() and (prediction > 0).all()
        raw_metrics = holdout_diagnostics(y_test, w_test, prediction)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(
            list(raw_metrics.values()), [run.models[name].metrics[k] for k in raw_metrics]
        )
        factor = op_ratio(y_train, train_prediction, w_train)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(op_ratio(y_train, factor * train_prediction, w_train), 1)
        adjusted = holdout_diagnostics(y_test, w_test, factor * prediction)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(adjusted["gini_test"], raw_metrics["gini_test"])
        for scale, values in [("raw", raw_metrics), ("training O/P adjusted", adjusted)]:
            appendix_rows.append({"model": name, "prediction_scale": scale,
                                  "training_factor": factor, **values})
for scale, table in pd.DataFrame(appendix_rows).groupby("prediction_scale", sort=False):
    print(scale)
    display(table.drop(columns="prediction_scale").set_index("model").rename(columns={
        "training_factor": "Factor", "gini_test": "Gini", "op_ratio_test": "O/P",
        "deviance_test": "Deviance", "d2_test": "D²",
    }))
print("All candidates on the raw scale")
display(comparison_table([*runs, *appendix_runs]).set_index("model")
        [["gini_test", "op_ratio_test", "deviance_test", "d2_test"]]
        .rename(columns={"gini_test": "Gini", "op_ratio_test": "O/P",
                         "deviance_test": "Deviance", "d2_test": "D²"}))
```

These are descriptive comparisons on one split, not evidence of statistical
superiority. The final table uses **raw** predictions for every candidate on the
same holdout; Tweedie deviance uses exposure weights and fixed power 1.5 (lower is
better), while O/P measures overall level and Gini measures concentration ranking.
The adjusted product rows above are a separate comparison scale.

In that same default render, the frequency–severity GLM has slightly lower raw
deviance than the direct Tweedie GLM (75.238 versus 75.338) and higher Gini (0.314
versus 0.310), but its overall O/P is farther from one (1.032 versus 1.022).
For raw-feature GBMs, the product has lower deviance (74.561 versus 74.721), but
slightly lower Gini (0.339 versus 0.342). Its raw O/P is still 1.174: observed
losses are 17.4% above predicted losses. Applying its frozen training factor once
brings held-out O/P to about 1.026; this does not establish segment calibration.
The component view helps explain what to investigate, while the product metrics
show the tradeoffs in the final price. Neither alternative improves every metric,
and this one split does not establish which model will perform best on future data.
